title: How Spain's migrant crisis created a political storm - whipped up by social media
description: Whatever the cause, Spain's socialist prime minister is angry with the response.Pedro Sanchez has hit out at some in the EU for "attacking" Spain in t
body: Whatever the cause, Spain's socialist prime minister is angry with the response.Pedro Sanchez has hit out at some in the EU for "attacking" Spain in this crisis, playing politics instead of showing support.He meant Italy, above all.Fratelli d'Italia, the hard-right party of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, had been quick to post images of migrants racing through the streets of Ceuta."This is the Sanchez model the Italian left wing likes so much," the caption crowed.Meloni then announced she was suspending Italy's Schengen agreement with Spain that allows for the free movement of people, citing a security threat.Madrid is fuming.The way Spain sees it, the crisis has been contained and Ceuta is not in the Schengen zone so Moroccan migrants were never going to head for mainland Europe, unchecked.Meloni knows that.But she faces elections next year with her coalition losing ground to a new and virulently anti-immigrant party. This was a chance to sound tough herself and claw back votes and she leaped on it.Italy is not the only country to see Spain as soft on migration, though.Meloni's call for an urgent meeting of interior ministers to be held on Tuesday was signed by almost two dozen EU heads of state, calling for the elimination of all policies that could be "pull factors" to Europe.Above all, they mean Spain's controversial move to allow hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants apply for residence and work permits and "regularise" their status.The government's pragmatic: Spain is ageing and needs workers.But those who flocked to the beaches of Ceuta this week were not heading to sign up for a campaign that's already closed.Sanchez himself points instead to a recent ruling by Spain's Supreme Court: it said those who enter by sea cannot be pushed back immediately.The prime minister argues that was misrepresented by smugglers to promise an easy path to Europe.The crowd heading for Ceuta didn't need to pay smugglers, though, because most were Moroccan and the route is well known.The message was actually spread online.Migrants have shown social media posts to reporters with people shouting that "Spain is Open" and jumping into the sea.Multiple accounts we've checked ourselves show young people in wetsuits and flippers, or filming themselves already swimming, mixed with pictures from inside Ceuta itself.Some have only been active for weeks. Several have tens of thousands of likes.All their promises were false.The crowds who made it to kiss the shore in Ceuta with joy were met with nothing. Without food or shelter, and with no way on to continental Europe, most quickly turned back.So have migrants been "weaponised" as happened a few years back in Belarus, for example?If so, who did it?For now we only see those enjoying the results.The global right wing are "hyperventilating with happiness", as journalist Andrea Rizzi wrote in Spain's El Pais newspaper.US President Donald Trump, angry at Spain for opposing his war on Iran, has talked of a "catastrophe" and an "invasion". Like Meloni, he has an election looming.Russia has been gloating, too: it loves chaos and division in Europe. Anything to weaken Ukraine's allies.As for Morocco, it's blaming "criminal organisations". But its border guards must have seen the crowds building.The last time something similar happened, albeit smaller, Spain and Morocco were at loggerheads over Western Sahara, a former colony.There are new tensions, right now.Sanchez is emphatically not blaming Morocco for what happened, calling Rabat a "good ally".But his critics call that appeasement and say he should be "showing teeth".

schema.headline: How Spain's migrant crisis created a political storm - whipped up by social media

title: Gianni Infantino: What next for Fifa and its under-pressure president?
description: A week is a long time in politics. Football politics. On Tuesday morning, Gianni Infantino was in an impregnable position as Fifa president, the most
body: A week is a long time in politics. Football politics. On Tuesday morning, Gianni Infantino was in an impregnable position as Fifa president, the most powerful job in football.Now, after trying to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investments firms - apparently without the knowledge of anyone else - Infantino's position appears to be under threat. Uefa - Infantino's fiercest critic - dealt its trump card on Thursday by threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.Now European football's governing body senses the opportunity to remove Infantino - and this is likely to be the best chance it will ever get.But they're far from the only unhappy federation. Concacaf, the confederation Infantino worked so closely with to organise the 2026 World Cup, has called for a "full review" into the leadership of Fifa in light of Infantino's plan. Even more damaging, loyal countries in the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) shunned him too.Then he was abandoned by two of his closest allies - first senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro and then chief operating officer Kevin Lamour.After Infantino backtracked in the early hours of Saturday morning, Uefa delivered another devastating blow by issuing a strong statement saying it had lost confidence in him.The battles lines have been drawn. What could happen next?The quickest route for Infantino's exit would be for the Swiss to resign, like his predecessor Sepp Blatter did in 2015. But Infantino still retains support and he could try to hold out until March, when he is up for re-election for a fourth and final term as president. What other avenues are open?The Fifa Council could try to force Infantino's hand through an emergency meeting.Such a gathering would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one.Uefa has nine members, AFC has seven, Concacaf five, Africa has six, Conmebol five and Oceania three. It is completed by Infantino and secretary general Mattias Grafstrom.BBC Sport understands there are some doubts that the 19 votes could be achieved. If they do get to 19, the meeting must take place within two weeks and the Fifa Council could call on Infantino to tender his resignation. But he could simply refuse to do so. It would, however, add further pressure.The next step would be an extraordinary congress of the 211 Fifa member associations, which would be held if one-fifth, or 43 associations, "make such a request in writing".So Uefa, which has 55 nations, can trigger the extraordinary congress whenever it wishes.That would take a minimum of two months from the point it is triggered, but more likely three months, and there is no guarantee of success.In effect, it would be a de facto election without there being another candidate as 106 votes would be needed to pass the vote of no confidence. Uefa has 55, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.Africa, Conmebol and Oceania have not criticised Infantino's plan.So could Uefa get to 106? In total, 136 countries officially rejected the investment plan, but voting to reject an idea is not the same as voting to kick Infantino out.Of the 136, Qatar have already publicly backed him and Mexico have distanced themselves from the joint Concacaf statement. Which leaves finding a suitable candidate to fight the election in March.Infantino stood unopposed when he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and if someone wants to battle him for the position, the deadline to announce their candidacy is 18 November.If Uefa and Infantino's biggest critics have to go down the election route, they will need to find a unifying leader.As Uefa has been so strong in its opposition to Infantino, a European candidate might struggle to get global support. After all, it might seem like it is trying to take over Fifa itself.So there must be a candidate who can attract the support of those countries in Concacaf, Africa and Asia who could have been loyal to Infantino but could be persuaded to switch their votes.The most likely candidate appears to be Concacaf president Victor Montagliani.Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to and delivery of the 2026 World Cup. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.Another option would be Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa, the AFC president.Initially elected in 2013, he was re-elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.Sheikh Salman signed off the confederation's brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.Less likely appears to be Paris St-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Qatari who is also the chair of European Football Clubs.Al-Khelaifi helped bring European football back together after another seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League.In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. Qatar's support for Infantino could be an issue, too.In any other business, Infantino would be unlikely to continue in his role. But football, of course, is not a normal business. Remember, Blatter had been re-elected the week before he resigned in 2015 when he had no option left amid a corruption scandal.So will Infantino try to fight on?In his statement on Saturday, he said his intent "was to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks". For Infantino, contrition could make this all float away.Maybe it is working. Following on from Qatar, 2030 co-hosts Morocco backed him on Saturday evening. Then Egypt praised Infantino for cancelling his masterplan.Infantino may be thinking that if he can, day by day, get more member associations on board, the prospect of a no-confidence vote is less likely to be successful. After all, his support base has been so strong for so long you can understand why he might have such faith. As any vote of no confidence is three months away, he has the chance to repair at least some of the damage.It is a race to 106 - and the more time elapses, the more chance Infantino can persuade his former allies this was just an aberration. For Uefa, the question is whether it can create a situation whereby Infantino is left with no option but to resign. For that to happen, the criticism from federations across the world must continue.But if there is one thing that could damage Infantino further, it would be for major sponsors to distance themselves from the organisation.During the 2015 Fifa scandal, Sony, Emirates, Castrol, Continental Tyres and Johnson & Johnson were among the companies to discontinue their huge sponsorship deals.There is no sign of this just yet but this is a saga with the potential to rumble on.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: What next for Fifa and its under-pressure president?

title: 'We are not lonely': Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle
description: Image source, @lanasololife/@dramafreediaries/@devonandwilloImage caption, Content creators sharing the peace of solo living is making the rounds on s
body: Image source, @lanasololife/@dramafreediaries/@devonandwilloImage caption, Content creators sharing the peace of solo living is making the rounds on social mediaByYang TianIt's a Friday night. A young woman trudges back to her apartment after a day of work. She enters a spotless kitchen, unloads a bag of groceries, and unwraps a frozen pizza before sliding it in the oven.What follows is a nightly routine that is almost meditative in its mundanity: she lights a candle and gazes briefly at the snow-covered landscape outside her window, piles a premade salad onto a plate with the pizza, and settles on her sofa to eat in front of the TV.The tagline that accompanies the scene reads: "POV you're a childfree and single girl that has no friends and lives alone so this is how you spend your Friday night."At the centre of the video – which has amassed seven million views on TikTok – is Lana Isa, a software sales manager in her 20s based in Toronto. In addition to chronicling her nightly self-care routines, she takes her almost 400,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram on late-night fast food drives, reading sessions perched on a rock by the lake, even a saga of getting locked out of her apartment in the middle of the night. Isa is part of a growing, albeit niche corner of the internet where content creators, many of them women, share their daily rituals of living alone, choosing to spotlight a lifestyle that prioritises peace and solitude - the antithesis of social media excess.For Isa, unveiling the "no friends" aspect of her life was less of a tagline, but the "reality" she had been living for several years.Alone, but not lonelyImage source, @lanasololifeImage caption, Lana Isa says her videos show her real life and were never intended to "romanticise having no friends"After switching several high schools, enduring Covid isolation during her college years and moving across the country following her first heartbreak, Isa found herself forced to adjust to living alone with no close friends."People don't talk about having no friends a lot... I think it's still what people would consider embarrassing or a little taboo," she says.When she started sharing the friendlessness of her circumstances on social media, an audience began to connect. Her initial following of around 2,000 followers on TikTok swelled to more than 175,000 in the span of eight months."It was eye-opening to see other people who are living the same situation that I've been… and to feel like I could kind of relate to people for the first time in a while."And relate they did. Isa's comments section filled with people bonding over similar experiences of living alone or having no friends, and finding comfort in "feeling seen".Figure caption, Alone not lonely: Meet the women building community through solitudeAs with most trends online, curiosity quickly turned to backlash. Isa and similar creators were dubbed "loneliness influencers", with some framing them as part of a new demographic of sad, lonely, childless women in crisis. Others accused them of romanticising self isolation and encouraging an "air of cosy defeatism" by shunning social connections.But their reels paint a lifestyle that may be more relatable than many would care to admit. These women take themselves on solo dates, embark on spontaneous road trips, and even push through the awkwardness of attending parties alone.Destigmatising lonelinessFor Devon Noehring, a full-time content creator and self-proclaimed introvert based in Phoenix, Arizona, it's been "frustrating" to see her solo weekends cooking and lounging at home with her dog reduced to a symptom of female loneliness."It's the exact opposite intention of our videos," she says. "I just hate the stigma of alone equalling lonely."While Noehring does have a close group of friends, growing up she always felt "ashamed" of being the quiet girl with social anxiety. It wasn't until she confessed her insecurities online that she discovered a following of fellow introverts who identified with her struggles."Being alone is where I feel my most free and most like myself," she says. "That's how I recharge, and I feel very proud of myself for being independent and doing things alone… I think it's something that should be celebrated."Image source, @devonandwilloImage caption, Devon Noehring says her content is about prioritising her peace and asks, "What about this is sad to you?"Some health researchers have been working to "destigmatise loneliness" by differentiating between chronic loneliness forced by circumstance and those who have agency to choose to live and spend time alone."Everybody's lonely at some point, but some people are not OK admitting that," says Professor Melody Ding, an epidemiologist researching social connection and loneliness at the University of Sydney. "That can create this false expectation that you have to be socially happy and connected all the time."But she cautions that while influencers can make being alone look "really appealing", humans still need social connection and it can be detrimental to one's mental and physical wellbeing to be stuck in a cycle of intense isolation."We're a social species," says Ding. "We survive better with companionship, with people around us."She acknowledges that people's social needs vary at different stages of life, but Ding's hope for those who have lost relationships is that they can eventually "de-emphasise" the friendless aspect of their lives and forge new social bonds."It's important we have people in our life and it's important these relationships are positive and nourish our lives," Ding adds.'We want to find people we relate to'Even in moments when they do feel lonely, these women say loneliness doesn't define their lives, nor do they aspire to remain permanently friendless."We never describe ourselves as lonely," says SJ Hoadley, who works as a cleaner in the UK and began documenting her own solo living after discovering Isa's videos. "I think sometimes my lack of friends tends to bother the people around me more than it bothers me."After leaving a seven-year abusive relationship, she moved to a new area where she knew no one and was confronted with having to rebuild her life. Despite the initial "shock", she eventually started "enjoying and embracing that independence" and "getting to feel comfortable with my own company".Image source, @dramafreediariesImage caption, SJ Hoadley calls herself an "accidental influencer" and never expected to gain such a huge followingIn a social media ecosystem that thrives on flooding our feeds with aspirational living and a perennial state of FOMO (fear of missing out), the rise of solo living influencers can be validating for those who see themselves reflected in the lifestyle, says Dr Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch at the University of Connecticut who specialises in how humans build community online."There's been this kind of long growing backlash against the idea that we're seeing everybody's perfect life, their highlight reel," she says.Oeldorf-Hirsch believes the appeal of solitude content is filling a social need for the creators and their audience, providing some "balance" against the dominance of hyper-glamourised influencer culture."We're kind of trending towards these influencers that are more authentic, living their true life," she says. "We just want to find people we relate to."Hoadley has seen her following surge at times by tens of thousands per day, while Noehring's videos have garnered millions of views across her channels.Those online connections have made Hoadley excited for a future where she finds a "little group of girlfriends". Noehring hopes to one day organise a real world meet-up with her virtual community, and Isa says the support has given her the "push" she needed to start thinking about making friends again."I think that what all the content is saying is: find your path," says Hoadley. "It doesn't have to be this one-size-fits-all that we keep getting pushed on social media."

schema.headline: 'We are not lonely': Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle

title: The 10 most overcrowded train services revealed
description: The most overcrowded train service in England and Wales last autumn was a Thameslink morning rush hour service between Bedford and Three Bridges in We
body: The most overcrowded train service in England and Wales last autumn was a Thameslink morning rush hour service between Bedford and Three Bridges in West Sussex, according to the Department for Transport (DfT).Second on the list was a West Midlands service from London Euston to Crewe, Cheshire, departing at 17:46, the government figures reveal. Overall, they show overcrowding on commuter trains serving major English and Welsh cities fell slightly, for the first time since 2020, due to an increase in capacity.Only 1.1% of peak-time travellers were on an overcrowded train, the DfT said. More than 1.2 million of the average 1.9 million journeys on a typical autumn day were in London.The DfT says work is under way to improve capacity where there are pinch points during peak hours.The Thameslink service which topped the list had a "load factor" – meaning how full the train was – of 176% at London St Pancras shortly after 08:00.The West Midlands service to Crewe had a load factor of 170%. It was busiest when it departed Euston.The third most crowded train was a Transport for Wales service from Bridgend to Rhymney, with a load factor of 161%. It was busiest at Llanishen.Four of the top ten services were operated by South Western, and Thameslink appeared twice more.Thameslink: Bedford to Three Bridges via London St Pancras (176% at 08:09)West Midlands: London Euston to Crewe (170% at 17:46)Transport for Wales: Bridgend to Rhymney via Llanishen (161% at 16:45)South Western: Alton to London Waterloo (159% at 08:22)Thameslink: Bedford to Three Bridges via London St Pancras (155% at 08:24)South Western: Fareham to London Waterloo via Vauxhall (151% at 08:19)Thameslink: Epsom to London Bridge (150% at 08:28)South Western: Portsmouth Harbour to London Waterloo via Vauxhall (149% at 08:27)South Western: London Waterloo to Basingstoke via Vauxhall (147% at 17:50)West Midlands: London Euston to Birmingham New Street (146% at 17:56)The DfT figures were based on passenger counts taken on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays between September and December 2025, and represent travel on a typical autumn weekday.Overcrowding fell slightly overall compared with autumn 2024, with an average of 16,800 (1%) passengers a day travelling in excess of capacity.The DfT said seating capacity has grown 4% in the past year.A spokesperson said: "The vast majority of passengers – 98.9% – typically travel on services that are not overcrowded."Where there are pinch points during peak hours, work is under way to improve capacity. GTR has added carriages to its busiest commuter services, while South Western Railway has boosted capacity by nearly 30% in the last year with new trains. "Bringing track and train together under Great British Railways will support further improvements, helping create a joined-up service that puts passengers first."A quarter of passengers travelling in and out of London at peak times had to stand. But in other cities, only 5% of passengers could not get a seat.A Thameslink spokesperson said its trains were designed to have ample standing room on board its busiest commuter routes."We are always monitoring how busy our services are and continually make changes to provide more space."In the last few years alone, we've lengthened trains on some of our busiest Bedford to London services and introduced an additional peak-time service to provide more choice and extra space."

schema.headline: The 10 most overcrowded train services revealed

title: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou have the choice of instantly receiving £50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of £1
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou have the choice of instantly receiving £50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of £1m.Which would you choose?The vast majority decide on taking the £50k, according to a survey of thousands of people by YouGov. Women voted 82% in favour of the guaranteed cash.The poll has sparked a debate about why Brits appear more risk-averse than people in the US.So why are the results so clear-cut, and what are the financial and psychological factors at play? Sadly, there is little chance of ever having such a choice, but there are some interesting lessons for how we manage our money nonetheless.Do you agree with the majority?Does the choice depend on how much you earn?Lots of people might opt for the £50,000 guarantee, deciding that it is a life-changing amount of money in itself.After all, it is £10,000 more than the median average earnings for full-time workers in the UK for an entire year, according to official statistics, external.But younger people generally earn less and yet, according to this survey, external, those aged 18 to 24 are more willing to take the bet on £1m than any other age group.Some 28% go for the coin flip, compared with just 11% among the over-65s - their grandparents' generation.There is a different tipping point for everyone. Repeat the survey but instead guarantee £5 or offer a 50/50 chance for a £100, and most people will probably go for the £100 bet. After all, lots of people bet at least £2 a week hoping for a National Lottery win.As those amounts rise, so your appetite for risk becomes clear.Why not just invest the £50k?One choice is to take the guaranteed £50,000 and hope it grows over time. Saving the money would be helped by the magic of compound interest.Alternatively, you could take more of a risk, but potentially with greater reward, by investing the money.What has happened in the past will not necessarily happen in the future when it comes to investments.But you'd have had to have invested your £50,000 in a typical global fund just under 38 years ago for it to be worth £1m today, according to Sarah Coles, of investment firm AJ Bell.Is it all in the mind?We are hardwired, says Coles, to go for the guaranteed £50,000.That's because we feel losses more acutely than gains, she says. "The thrill of potentially winning £1m is felt less strongly than the fear of giving up a guaranteed £50,000 and ending up with nothing," she says.In other words, having £50k and knowing you might have won £1m will play on your mind.But it is not as bad as having a crack at £1m and knowing you've given up enough for an average deposit to buy a home in the West Midlands, external.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Josh Kerr wins Saturday night scrap in Glasgow
description: There were no pacers. No wave lights. No declarations about what time he would run or what record he would beat. This was a Saturday night scrap - Gla
body: There were no pacers. No wave lights. No declarations about what time he would run or what record he would beat. This was a Saturday night scrap - Glasgow rules - and Josh Kerr wasn't going to let anyone beat him in that fight. Not his childhood pal and Scotland team-mate Jake Wightman. Not the Australian prodigy Cam Myers. Not the former Olympic silver medallist Timothy Cheruiyot. This Commonwealth Games men's mile was his race, in his country, in front of his people. This gold medal really meant something. Kerr's explosion of joy after he crossed the line and swaddled himself in a Saltire - having conducted the crowd during his final few strides - made that clear. And so did his halting attempts to sing along with Flower of Scotland, the 28-year-old repeatedly stopping to bite his lip before wiping away tears from each eye. "We rush through these moments so quickly," Kerr told BBC Sport Scotland, having spent the best part of 45 minutes doing selfies and signatures. "So I was just telling myself to slow down. "In my head, I was flashing through all the hard moments and realising that I've come a long way. And to have Flower of Scotland playing versus the GB national anthem, it's just different. Not many times in my career I'll ever have that."When Kerr crossed the line, the clock showed he was almost eight seconds slower than when running the fastest time ever for the mile in London last month. Three minutes 54.12 seconds.What it didn't show was that for three of the four laps, this was more rammy than race.   Emerging between fireworks, Kerr had strutted out on to the track, spinning a bottle, and allowed his 12 rivals to sprint away. Only once they checked and began to run back did he stretch his own legs and acknowledge the crowd. Aura.The Scot also made sure to position himself between Myers and Cheruiyot on the start line. A flex, perhaps, but why not? Kerr has the credentials, after all. Former world champion, Olympic silver and bronze, the big dog in this fight.And he needed all of his snarl and bite to survive the three laps of jostling, barging and bumping that followed. The race was slow, too slow. And physical, really physical. Could Kerr - trapped in the pack, pinned to the kerb - deal with that? "As long as you stay on your feet, it's fine," was his assessment afterwards. At the time, Kerr gave his answer as the bell tolled. In a flash, he made his move, bursting to the outside in pursuit of Myers and Cheruiyot, who made theirs momentarily first. With 250m to go, Kerr left them behind. Wightman gamely tried to follow but how do you chase down a man this fast? His brave gamble failed and the bronze medallist from the last two Games trailed home in sixth.By then, Kerr was already celebrating gold, with Myers coming through for silver and Cheruiyot bronze. "I peeked up at the screen, saw I had a bit of a gap, and I felt great," added the Edinburgh athlete, who has been racing at Scotstoun since he was a child. "I was just trying to stay present and enjoy it. I learned how to race on that track - and I've had some pretty bad ones out there - so to really enjoy that last 100m was a really important moment."It was the moment Glasgow 2026 has been building to. The historic, reinstated, Blue Riband event of these Games got a fittingly elite winner. As a student of the sport's history, Kerr will appreciate that. And as a kid who was at the athletics event at Hampden in 2014, he knew how much joy every man, women and child inside this place would derive from every picture he had taken, every word he shared with them, and every scrawl of his name."I have to take my time out there because they've waited and put their hard-earned money to come out and watch me perform," he said."You've got to stay in your lane and realise I'm lucky coming into this championship healthy, ready to go and I'm in the best shape of my life. And to do that in front of a home crowd is very special."

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Josh Kerr wins Saturday night scrap in Glasgow

title: Penarth woman, 86, orphaned as child raises funds for charityafter childhood promise to herself
description: A woman who grew up as an orphan and promised to "help any child I could" has spent 30 years opening her picturesque garden to visitors to raise money
body: A woman who grew up as an orphan and promised to "help any child I could" has spent 30 years opening her picturesque garden to visitors to raise money for a children's charity. Ann Lush, 86, was raised alongside her brother by her grandmother, who was widowed during World War Two, and said her childhood inspired her lifelong commitment to helping young people.Lush, from Penarth, said she had promised herself: "If I ever had a home of my own, everybody could come to it."She has now raised more than £130,000 for The Children's Society through Penarth Open Gardens, which she started with her late husband Dennis in 1996, charging £1 per head to enter her garden.Dozens of gardens are now included in the event each year.Lush said that when she was young, her grandmother would not let her invite friends to the house, but that friends' parents had done the opposite. "I resolved when I was about nine years of age... that I would help any child I could as I got older," she told BBC Radio Wales. "And if I ever had a home of my own, everybody could come to it," said Lush, who has received an MBE alongside her husband for their charity work. "And everybody has come to it. Not just through the open gardens, because I've had strawberry teas, I've had barbecues, I've had garage sales. "It's been a wonderful thing to be able to do with my garden. It really, really has," she said.

schema.headline: Penarth woman, 86, orphaned as child raises funds for charityafter childhood promise to herself

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: England beaten by Australia to netball bronze
description: England's netballers were beaten 68-50 by world number one side Australia in their quest to win bronze at the Commonwealth Games.The day after Saturda
body: England's netballers were beaten 68-50 by world number one side Australia in their quest to win bronze at the Commonwealth Games.The day after Saturday morning's frustrating semi-final loss to New Zealand, England tried to rally themselves to get on the podium but came up against a Diamonds team recovering from one of the biggest shocks in the tournament's history.Australia - who had previously been in every Commonwealth final and won the tournament four times - were stunned by Jamaica on Saturday afternoon, giving them less time to recover for the bronze-medal match than England.The crowd responded to a lively start as great pressure from Roses captain Fran Williams led to Australia shooter Kiera Austin missing a shot with the score at 5-5, and Liv Tchine neatly slotted the ball in to open up a lead at the other end.England worked hard to shut down the Diamonds' forward-passing options, forcing them to play sideways, but the team in green and gold found their rhythm with devastating consequences, overturning a 9-7 deficit to lead 19-11 in a bruising seven-minute first-quarter spell for the Roses.Anna Stembridge's side, who lost 66-47 to the same opponents in the pool stage, then lacked impetus in the second period, showing signs of tired legs against one of the world's most established shooting partnerships in Austin and Sophie Garbin.A loose pass from Williams sent the ball straight into Australia's hands, allowing Austin to calmly extend the gap to 28-16 and her side kept the margin steady, resulting in a half-time score of 35-24.With Australia leading by 16 points in the third quarter, England rolled the dice by bringing on shooter Eleanor Cardwell for Tchine, and her presence helped the Roses score five without reply to trail 45-34 and then 49-36 with 15 minutes left to play.Bronze is not a colour of medal that Australia ever imagined they would be playing for, but what seemed just as important to them was reminding the world what they are capable of and why they have been such feared opponents.In that respect, Stacey Marinkovich's Diamonds shone as ultimate professionals, and England again came up short against a top side, losing by one less point than the pool stage match between the teams.Jamaica - who have never won netball gold at the Games - will play two-time champions New Zealand in Sunday afternoon's gold-medal match (13:00).

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: England beaten by Australia to netball bronze

title: Why more men in their 20s are having vasectomies
description: Why I don't regret choosing a vasectomy in my 20sImage source, Alex WestImage caption, Alex West says he remembers the months after the births of his
body: Why I don't regret choosing a vasectomy in my 20sImage source, Alex WestImage caption, Alex West says he remembers the months after the births of his two sons as "grey"ByGeorge SandemanAlex West was left harrowed by the difficult labour his wife endured for their first child. When it came to their second, he hoped for a much smoother arrival.The birth did go better for his wife - but not for him. "I had a panic attack and broke down. I hadn't been able to - I didn't have the ability to - process that," Alex says.Unresolved trauma from his wife's first labour and his subsequent postnatal depression meant Alex didn't want to continue with the couple's plan to have four children.He remembers the months after the births of his two sons as "grey" - life was devoid of colour and filled with people telling him that being a father must be a fantastic experience."I didn't feel this love and connection that everybody says I should have," Alex says.Not wanting to repeat the experience, he and his wife agreed to stop at two kids. Given he was the driving force behind the decision, he felt it was "wrong to put the onus on my wife" to take a contraceptive.So like thousands more men in England have done in recent years, Alex chose to have a vasectomy.The procedure involves the cutting and then clamping or sealing of the vas deferens, a tube on each testicle that carries sperm to the urethra. It's colloquially known as the snip.Figure caption, How a vasectomy worksSome 26,385 vasectomies were performed at hospitals and clinics during 2024-25, according to data compiled by NHS England. This was 16% more than in 2023-24.Men aged 35-39 had more procedures than any other age group, about 8,400 in 2024-25.There had also been a slight rise on the previous year in younger men choosing to have the snip - about 950 vasectomies were performed on men aged under 30 in England during 2024-25.Fears about pregnancyAlex, a mortgage broker, decided in his late 20s to have the procedure but his NHS doctor urged him to wait until he turned 30 in case he changed his mind.When the appointment came in May 2024, he and his wife took the train from their Kent home to the London clinic.The procedure was quick and painless says Alex, now 33. "I put my headphones on and I listened to about three songs before they said it was all done."Ridiculous - crazy quick."Image source, Sam KnightImage caption, Sam Knight decided to have a vasectomy after a woman he was dating became pregnantSam Knight, who's from the US, says he knew he didn't want to have children."I was putting myself in situations where kids could be a potential option and that really started to, kind of, freak me out," Sam says. When his then-partner became pregnant, she chose to have an abortion and Sam, aged 22 at the time, felt a change was needed."[I had] a realisation of this thing that I've put somebody through and I just didn't want that to ever happen again."He contacted a urology clinic in New York and, like Alex, had to explain to clinicians why he wanted a vasectomy. Sam was advised the procedure should be treated as permanent, as it can only be reversed in some circumstances.Strict criteria for reversals Because he was asking for a vasectomy at such a young age, Sam had prepared for the questions his doctor was going to ask him: Don't you think you're too young to know you don't want kids? Could you change your mind in future? You do know reversals are expensive and aren't always successful?"[The doctor] actually said he had very recently changed his view," says Sam. "And that, if I had come in half a year earlier, he would have turned me away instantly."His vasectomy took place a couple of months after he first contacted the clinic.The questions from Sam's doctor were designed to ensure he was making a decision he could live with; men under 30 are more likely to regret a vasectomy, according to guidance from NHS Scotland, external.Dr Sarah Salkeld, a former GP who is now a medical director for MSI Reproductive Choices, a group of clinics offering various contraceptives to NHS and private patients, says a vasectomy is "very safe and effective".But she cautions it is important for men to "really think about" whether a vasectomy is right for them."We offer everyone counselling to talk about it if they want to, just to… make sure they've got all the information they need to make that decision." She says reversals are not routinely available on the NHS as there are strict criteria for having one. The NHS website points out that other forms of contraception, external are available to men, including condoms and the fertility awareness method - avoiding sex or using condoms on the days when their female partner is most fertile.Sam told his doctor that, while he loved kids and had a happy childhood himself, he wanted to stay focused on his job as a sound designer for video games.Image source, Alex WestImage caption, Alex and his wife initially planned to have four kids but after careful consideration stopped at two"I've devoted my life to this and, to me, parenting is something you also devote your life to," Sam says. "I just don't have the mental space or the time to do that, or even the desire to."Sam, now 25, says he envies those who do want to become parents because the experience "clearly has" beauty and love in it. But adds, "I find that in music and art and these things that I do."The procedure in 2024 and the aftercare cost Sam, who was still on his family's health insurance policy, about $1,200 (£849) in total.He's among fewer than 1% of men in the US aged 18-29 who have ever had a vasectomy, according to the National Survey of Family Growth, which analysed the responses of about 4,000 men in 2022-23. Men in their mid to late 40s were most likely to have had one -15% said they had.Sacrifices and uncertainties of being a parent Sam experienced one bout of excruciating pain a week after the procedure, a known but uncommon side effect of vasectomies according to Dr Salkeld, but that subsided after a few hours.He doesn't think this should put other men off having a vasectomy. "Overall, it is worth the money and it is worth the pain," he says.Another man told us the sacrifices and uncertainties of being a parent - particularly how his children might turn out - drove him to have a vasectomy aged 27.Back in Kent, the decision to get the snip felt like the fairest and most effective form of contraception available to Alex and his wife.It was something they considered carefully over several months, knowing Alex didn't want to grow their family."I absolutely adore my children," Alex says, particularly now they are old enough to play football with."If I had added more to the team, it wouldn't have been the right thing for me."Get in touchWe are interested in hearing from men who have had a vasectomy reversal. What prompted your decision?

schema.headline: Why more men in their 20s are having vasectomies

title: Clacton by-election ballot list costing four times more
description: Davidson said his teams are having to make changes to the way they usually carry out elections.The ballots are "going to be sometimes longer than the
body: Davidson said his teams are having to make changes to the way they usually carry out elections.The ballots are "going to be sometimes longer than the table so we're having to do double tables and we're going to have to sort them in batches before we can verify them or even count them."Paul Whiteley, professor of government at the University of Essex, said the previous record for the number of candidates standing for a seat in the House of Commons was the Haltemprice and Howden by-election in East Yorkshire in July 2008."David Davis resigned his seat and stood again as a protest over the issue of civil liberties," explained Whiteley."There were 26 candidates."Prior to that, the previous record was the Newbury by-election in Berkshire in 1993, which featured 19 candidates.Farage resigned as MP for Clacton on 7 July, following increased scrutiny over his finances and a parliamentary investigation, but the Reform leader is standing again.Among the candidates on the ballot are 20 independents - also a record for a single  election.A full list of the 34 candidates is available on the BBC News website. The main parties have chosen not to stand.

schema.headline: Clacton by-election ballot list costing four times more

title: Fans praise 'mature' Tom Holland Spider-Man performance
description: Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superher
body: Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superhero.Spider-Man: Brand New Day marks Tom Holland's fourth standalone adventure as the protagonist and hero Peter Parker.Picking up after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the film follows Parker as he devotes his time to protecting New York City while adjusting to a life in which everyone, including his closest friends, has forgotten who he is.The fourth Spider-Man film is director Destin Daniel Cretton's second project in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), having previously been at the helm of Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings.Appearing together in the same film for a second time this summer, Holland reprises the role alongside his wife Zendaya, who stars once again as MJ.There is also a return for Jon Bernthal's Punisher, making his first appearance in an MCU feature film, and an introduction to the MCU for Sadie Sink, whose role in the plot has been kept firmly under wraps.The reviews from critics have been largely positive.Many critics have welcomed the film-makers' decision to scale back from the multiverse seen in No Way Home, in favour of a more personal, character-centred story. The Telegraph's Robbie Collin called it, external "the best Spider-Man film since the Tobey Maguire era", and praised the relationship between Holland and Zendaya, who create a "real yearning and perplexity" that we have not seen previously in the dynamic between their characters.In his review for The Wrap, William Bibbiani, external described it as the strongest entry in Holland's Spider-Man series, applauding its emotional focus and character-driven storytelling, and praising its "wonderful, propulsive quality".Meanwhile, Empire's John Nugent awarded the film four stars, external, declaring the web-slinging hero is "still Marvel's ace in the pack", and in its five-star review The Standard said the film had "verve, intelligence and above all, heart".However, others have been more reserved.The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw declared, external that Zendaya "saves this film" from "silliness and the generic déjà vu overfamiliarity that is always threatening to sink it".This opinion was supported by David Rooney in the Hollywood Reporter, external, who wrote that the film "chugs along satisfyingly even with the occasional patch of sluggishness and the usual overly convoluted plot contortions".He adds: "As much as the movie revels in the thrill of Spidey swinging between skyscrapers with erratic command of his shooters, the more intimate scenes with MJ and Ned are what supplies the emotional charge."Danny Leigh of the Financial Times awarded the film three stars, external, praising the chemistry between Holland and Zendaya but criticising the film's insistence on falling back on CGI-heavy action sequences.But that is just what the critics say. What do audiences think?Holland and Zendaya were just 20 and 19 years old, respectively, when they first met in 2016 on the set of Spider-Man: Homecoming, during the movie's casting and initial production.Ten years and multiple other blockbusters later, there is an ever-growing speculation that their futures now lie away from the MCU.Speaking on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, external with Josh Horowitz, Holland hinted that a new chapter was on the horizon, albeit not clarifying when."It's going to change, for sure", he said."There is a whole plan that we have been working on since, I would say, Spider-Man No Way Home."I have a really clear vision to the passing on of the baton, and I think it is really exciting."Zendaya and Tom Holland's decade-long Spider-Man romance in picturesAs for Zendaya, she has hinted previously that she is planning on taking a career break at the end of 2026, after a busy schedule that included the promotion of her films The Drama, The Odyssey, Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Dune: Part Three.Earlier this year Zendaya told Elle, external that "I think that after this, I'm going to have to take a little bit of a break".She backed this notion up when asked about her future plans, external by Entertainment Tonight at the NYC premiere of The Odyssey, replying, "Oh, girl, nothing. Just mind my business!".

schema.headline: Fans praise 'mature' Tom Holland Spider-Man performance

title: Trump says he is cancelling strikes on Iran subject to deal being made 'rapidly'
description: Donald Trump says he has cancelled strikes against Iran, provided a deal is struck "rapidly" with the country.In a post on Truth Social, the US presid
body: Donald Trump says he has cancelled strikes against Iran, provided a deal is struck "rapidly" with the country.In a post on Truth Social, the US president said he had been asked by Iran and other countries in the Middle East to "hold off" on any attack as the "perimeters" of a deal had been agreed. Trump's comments came after reports that the US and Israel may have been planning new, intense strikes on Iran.It is not the first time that Trump has issued apocalyptic warnings, only to subsequently insist that diplomacy was being given a chance. Iran has not confimed requesting new talks or any agreement on the outline of a deal to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on 28 February.On Sunday, Iran's acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza said Tehran viewed every threat from its adversaries as "real and credible" even if it formed part of psychological warfare."We will neither be caught off guard nor remain passive," he added.The raised tones followed reports in the US media that the US and Israel were planning what would be one of the harshest bombing campaigns to date against energy infrastructure targets in Iran. The plan came up during Trump's cabinet meeting on Friday, sources told CBS News, the BBC's News partner in the US.The US government had also urged Americans across the Middle East to be alert and ready to leave "should there be escalation" in the region.In his post on Saturday, Trump said the US was "locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II".He said cancelling the attack would be "for the future benefit of the world and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran".Back on 7 April, the US president warned that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" if Iran refused to engage in peace talks. He threatened to destroy civilian infrastructure and power plants, a move that many said would be a war crime.That threat did result in historic face-to-face talks in Pakistan, led by Vice President JD Vance. For supporters of the president, it was vindication. Bellicose threats - often referred to as the "Madman Theory" - resulted in talks with the Iranians.The issue with that view, however, is that those talks ended without a deal. There were simply too many competing red lines that could not be reconciled, even with the threat of civilisation erasure.During the Friday meeting, CBS News reported Trump was heard saying while reporters were still in the room: "We'll be hitting them [Iranians] very hard. At some point, they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore.'"A dau later, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had a call with Trump, aimed at reducing regional tensions, the kingdom's official SPA press agency reported."His Royal Highness emphasised the necessity of prioritising dialogue to reduce tensions and the importance of exerting all possible efforts to achieve a truce that paves the way for diplomatic solutions."The US's Gulf Allies hold concerns that, while the American mainland is out of reach of Iranian missiles, countries like Bahrain, Jordan and the United Arab Emirates are not - with their critical infrastructure such as water desalination plans being prime targets.Washington and Tehran have engaged in escalating strikes and counter-strikes since a ceasefire in April aimed at pausing the war fell apart in June.The US has blockaded Iranian ports and bombed Iranian sites, while Iran has fired missiles and drones at US assets in countries across the Middle East and targeted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global oil shipping.There have been significant fluctuations in oil prices since then.It is not only international pressure that the US president faces. According to the Pew research centre, around 60% of Americans disapprove of the war with Iran, contributing to Trump's falling popularity.Any escalation would almost certainly result in an increase in oil prices, further squeezing US consumers. With crucial US midterm elections looming, the president will know his international decisions could have serious domestic consequences for his administration.

schema.headline: Trump says he is cancelling strikes on Iran subject to deal being made 'rapidly'

title: Gingers of America - The Scot documenting the redheads of the US
description: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting AmericansImage source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Rosalie Moore is one of hundreds of
body: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting AmericansImage source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Rosalie Moore is one of hundreds of ginger-haired subjects Kieran has photographedBySteven BrocklehurstBBC ScotlandUpdated 1 hour agoFor Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade.The 45-year-old, from Edinburgh, who is himself a "proud ginger", began taking pictures in his homeland in 2013 as part of a series examining Scottish identity.His interest in the subject soon took him to other ginger hotspots such the Russian city of Perm and Jamaica's Treasure Beach.His 2020 book Gingers spanned the world but after its release he notice there was a "huge gap"."I realised I didn't have any American citizens," Kieran told the BBC. "Then all these people got in touch."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Nicholas Modaressi says his dad, who grew up in Iran, refuses to get his genetics tested. "I'm Persian," he tells his son Nic, who grew up in Maryland"I was like 'oh wow, of course, the whole world is in the States'," Kieran says. "It's a microcosm."He says a message from a Native American man who had red hair instantly aroused his curiosity."I found it very interesting and it made me think, 'where on earth did it come from?'"Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Joshua Elliot says his mum's side has always been involved with the Muscogee tribeThe cover of his latest book - Gingers of America, external - features Joshua Elliot from the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma.He told Kieran that some of his mother's relatives were German and on his dad's side there were people from England and Sweden, so that could explain where his ginger hair comes from. "My mom's side has always been involved with the Muscogee tribe and traditions and I've grown up around it," he said. Joshua knows he does not fit people's expectations of what a Native American should look like, but he said: "Our chief's wife told me it's about your involvement in your community and your tribe, the people around you and what you put back into it."Which I really took to heart." Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Lottie Wahkinney is a Comanche girl, from Oklahoma, with Scottish grandparentsKieran spoke to a lot of Native Americans on his visits and most knew of a European ancestry which could explain their red hair. "The thing that surprised me was how early on there were these Scots and Irish marrying Native Americans," he said.Lottie Wahkinney, a Comanche girl from Oklahoma, has Scottish grandparents, from Galashiels.Her father Jared told Kieran his dad was Comanche but his mum was born and raised in Scotland."That's why my Lottie has a good mix of everything going on," Jared said. "My Scottish grandparents would come over every summer. "On my first visit to Scotland when I was 22, folks were like, 'Where are your moccasins? Where's your headdress?'. "I explained 'I wear Nikes'."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Lakia Jones (right) says all her relatives have long, straight, jet-black hair like her sister Maci (left)While most Native Americans could explain where the ginger gene might have come from, there was one exception - a Cherokee girl called Lakia - whose family knew of no European ancestry."It is a totally different colour of red," Kieran said. "It's deep ruby. That really intrigued me." In the book, Lakia says that all her family, on both sides, have jet-black straight hair but hers turned red during her childhood."Everyone thought, since I was about eight, that I dyed my hair," she said. "And still now everyone's like, 'what hair colour is that?'."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Jaxston Hudson from Birmingham, AlabamaAfter meeting Native Americans, Kieran knew there was something in the US he could explore. Over the next few years, he made seven lengthy trips, often linked to his full-time profession as an environmental photographer.One state he found surprising was Alabama, a place many in the UK associate with racial segregation and the struggle for civil rights as well as its pioneering space exploration programmes."I knew it for racism and Nasa," Kieran said. "In my head it was stuck in the 60s but Birmingham is an incredibly vibrant city."I met a lot of black Americans who had often married someone who is white."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Rachel Releford says people think she is her daughter Liliana's nannyRachel Releford told Kieran that when she goes out with her daughter Liliana people think she is the nanny or the babysitter."I'm like, 'nope, she's mine'," Rachel said. "I think you still get some people who grew up with the mindset that things need to be segregated. "Some of my grandparents' friends were a little hesitant when they found out I was dating my husband. They said: 'You're really going to let her date someone of a different race?'"But my grandparents were like, 'Go for it. He's a cool guy, he's a sweet one.' I love him for who he is. He's a great human being."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption,  Henry Davis says he had red hair like his son when he was youngerAlso in Alabama, he met Henry Davis and his young son Henry Davis II.The older man no longer has any red hair but he says he looked just like his son when he was the same age."We're not really sure where it comes from," Henry senior said. "My dad is turning grey now. He'll get some red in his beard, and then it kind of goes grey. "So I guess it's from his side." Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Colton, Bennett, Emmeline, Christopher, Amelia, and Genevieve Smith from Burke, VirginiaAs someone who grew up with red hair himself, Kieran says he is well aware that ginger can be used as an insult.However, he says: "I use the word for its descriptive power because red is the colour of fire engines and blood whereas ginger has a golden tone to it. "You can use it in a kind way."He says the book uses ginger hair as "a golden thread" that weaves together America's diverse and difficult history in a way which shows a connection between people."That's my big idea," Kieran says."We are all made of the same stuff and with the ginger hair it shows."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Cali Trawick has an ancestry that includes Irish, African-American, indigenous American and Hispanic rootsAccording to Kieran no-one exemplifies this better than a young lad named Cali whom he met in Alabama."His background is everything - European, African-American, Hispanic and indigenous as well," he says. "His gran is white but she was unable to get married to a black guy in Alabama - even after the courts had made it legal. "She moved to Georgia and had a family there. It's an incredibly diverse family."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Allison Dubinski grew up in Indiana but says her hair colour is a key asset to help her stand out in the competitive acting world of New YorkIn Scotland, it is thought as many as 13% of the population - about 700,000 people - are natural redheads, a higher percentage than anywhere else in the world.Globally, less than 2% of the population are thought to have red hair but Kieran's research lead him to believe the US figure is higher than that. "We landed on about 4% for the genetic prevalence," he says."If all the gingers in America were gathered in one place, Gingertown would be about 14 million people. "It's a big city. You would see it from space it would be so bright."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Evelyn Lee, from Birmingham, Alabama, used to hate her ginger curls but now she loves them. "I think it's like Spanish princesses' flowing locks - like medieval paintings," she says. Kieran says the big difference between America and other places is that they tend to have really thought about where they come from."Everyone has self-consciously moved from somewhere," he says."And that includes the Native Americans, who have been moved from other parts of America."That's what makes it interesting."He says his book is a road trip through the US trying to find out about the country through this unique trait.Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Keisha Engley grew up in rural Washington State. Her American grandfather fought in Vietnam and met her grandmother there.For Kieran, the recent men's football World Cup got people excited about the US again in a way they haven't been over the past few years because of political divisions.He says he was pleased to see people visiting the US and saying "it is not what I expected"."There's such a lot of amazing people and communities there," he says. "People you might connect with and agree with on a lot of things."I'm quite heartened that the football has revealed that."I feel quite patriotic for America now."Image source, Kieran DoddsImage caption, Kieran says he has become quite patriotic for America

schema.headline: Gingers of America - The Scot documenting the redheads of the US

title: Peak District's rebrand deal brings in cash - but also criticism
description: Image source, Jessica PeachImage caption, The altered signs are promoting a new electric modelByGeorge TorrDerbyA deal between Peak District bosses an
body: Image source, Jessica PeachImage caption, The altered signs are promoting a new electric modelByGeorge TorrDerbyA deal between Peak District bosses and car firm Skoda to put up temporary signs welcoming tourists to "the Peaq District" in honour of the firm's new electric model has given the park authority's coffers a welcome boost.However, it has also sparked protests from campaigners and residents unhappy about the commercial aspect of the arrangement.One campaigner said: "If national parks are prepared to sell their very name to the highest bidder, then we're already on the path to industrial extraction of the most protected landscapes."Park bosses have defended the "fantastic" deal and said the partnership brought in extra funds for conservation and heritage work.With national parks continuing to grapple with funding pressures, could the partnership be a sign of things to come for the Peak District and beyond?Image caption, Phil Mulligan said the partnership aligned with the park's values and brought in much needed fundsAnnouncing the link-up, Skoda UK said the partnership was meant to "spark positive conversations" and to "encourage more people to get out and enjoy the Peak District in a responsible way". But campaigners are not convinced.They told the BBC the partnership had raised "broader questions" about how national parks were funded and whether "increasing financial pressures" were leading authorities to seek commercial partnerships that "conflict with their environmental purpose".National parks are primarily funded through the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), with the Peak District receiving £6m for 2025-26.According to the Campaign for National Parks, external, government funding for National Park Authorities was reduced by 9% in that financial year, which it said had contributed to an estimated 40% real-terms reduction in funding since 2010 at a time when visitor numbers "continue to reach record levels".The government says it is investing £37m in national parks over the next three years plus a further £30m for special habitats and species.Phil Mulligan, chief executive of the Peak District National Park Authority, said the temporary rebranding was "exciting" and the money would help conservation, heritage and access works. He declined to reveal the sum received but described it as a "reasonable amount".Image source, Jessica PeachImage caption, Campaigners say the brand deal raised further questions about funding for national parksCampaigner Harry Brook was part of a protest at one of the signs at Surprise View car park near Hathersage."I don't think what we have seen recently in the Peak District National Park is anyone's vision for the future of our national parks," he told the BBC."If you've had a sugar high, you're likely to go back again, aren't you?"Brook added he "wholeheartedly sympathised" with Mulligan and said there was a lack of funding going into national parks.However, he said: "It's silly we are at the point where we are having to resort to this type of funding to back national parks."Phil's said it himself, we're in a climate and biodiversity crisis, we know investing in our national parks is a strategic investment, so why are we having to resort to on the 75th anniversary of the park to selling the rights to the name?"These landscapes are not there for commodification." Image caption, Campaigner Harry Brook said the partnership was systematic of a much broader issue around fundingAsked whether he anticipated the negative response from some residents, Mulligan said he did because people were "passionate about the national park"."The national park brings wonderful benefits to the nation and how it's here for everyone and how it's free for everyone," he said."But unfortunately, it's not free to deliver and with a declining government grant, we always seek to work in partnership with others."This Skoda promotion, I think, is fantastic... we're not actually changing the name of the national park, it's a one-week promotion. "It allows us to receive a financial contribution that we can put to conservation, heritage, access works, so it's really positive."While I understand some people will have some concerns about it, it's quite standard really to have a very temporary digital takeover and I think it's for the enhancement and betterment of the national park and visitors."Image caption, Dawn Fleetham said the partnership did not fit with the Peak DistrictVisitors approached by the BBC at Surprise View were both for and against the deal.Dawn Fleetham disagreed with the rebranded sign."I don't think they should be doing that to the Peak District - somehow it just doesn't fit," she said.A male visitor said: "I'm against some of the capitalist, advertisment stuff - it's like the same with football stadiums being named after brands. Having the traditional names is better in my opinion. "I know they're giving [the park] money so it's good but it's a hard one."Image caption, James Dawson said he found the rebranding peculiarAnother visitor disagreed, sating: "It's just one sign... I think it's good advertising. It gets seen a lot."But James Dawson said: "I thought it was a bit peculiar, the Peak isn't spelt that way, it's not spelt with a Q."I don't know what relevance Skodas have with the Peak District."Image source, National Parks PartnershipsImage caption, Santander UK funded the restoration of 220 hectares of damaged peatland in three national parksThis is not the first time a corporate brand has partnered with a national park.In the face of growing funding pressures, National Park Partnerships, external was established in 2016 specifically to create commercial relationships with places like the Peak District.The partnerships fund conservation, visitor access, climate and community projects while allowing brands to associate themselves with protected landscapes.One recent example is BMW UK, which formed a three-year "Recharge In Nature" partnership with national parks in 2022.The aim was to to enhance the electric vehicle (EV) charging network across all 15 parks in the UK, while supporting a range of projects including nature restoration, biodiversity, regenerative tourism, and wellbeing initiatives.Other brands involved with partnerships on conservation projects include high street bank Santander UK, mobile phone networks Vodafone and Three, and beauty giant Estée Lauder.Image source, National Parks EnglandImage caption, Debbie Stockwell said national parks needed to be "innovative" on how they raised moneyNational Parks England executive director, Debbie Stockwell, said authorities needed to be "innovative" to raise money from a "range of sources"."We welcomed the funding settlement from central government for 2026-2027, which enables national park authorities to deliver core services and projects," she said."However, over the last decade, the national park authorities that maintain these cherished places have faced the challenges of reduced central funding and rising costs. "We are committed to diversifying our funding, and National Parks Partnership has been established to secure corporate and philanthropic giving. "National Parks need to be innovative to raise income from a range of sources and were recently given increased powers by government in order to do this."Additional reporting by Ian Skye and Rachel RoyceGet in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Derby

schema.headline: Peak District's rebrand deal brings in cash - but also criticism
